paragraphs.heading: Quotient and remainder
paragraphs.text: Dividing a polynomial A by another polynomial B gives two results: a quotient Q and a remainder R. The remainder is either zero or has a lower degree than B. Those conditions settle Q and R completely, so there is only one such pair. Finding that pair is called Euclidean division, and polynomial long division is a step-by-step method for carrying it out.

paragraphs.heading: A test for factors
paragraphs.text: The remainder comes out zero exactly when B is a factor of A. That makes long division a way to test whether one polynomial divides another, and to pull the factor out when it does. The method works as long as the coefficients come from one field, a number system where you can always divide by anything that is not zero. The rational, real and complex numbers are all fields.

paragraphs.heading: Working one example
paragraphs.text: Take x³ − 2x² − 4, the dividend, divided by x − 3, the divisor. First divide the leading term of the dividend by the highest-power term of the divisor: x³ ÷ x = x², which goes above the bar. Multiply the divisor by x² to get x³ − 3x², write it under the first two terms, and subtract, which leaves x². Bring down the next term and repeat the same three steps on the new line. The finished line above the bar is the quotient, and the number left at the bottom, 5, is the remainder.

paragraphs.heading: Cousins of the method
paragraphs.text: Long division of ordinary numbers works in nearly the same way, with x replaced by 10 and every coefficient kept non-negative. When the divisor has the form x − c, a shortcut called synthetic division needs less writing and fewer calculations. It lays the coefficients of the dividend in the top row of a three-row table. The leading coefficient drops to the bottom row, gets multiplied by c, and the result is written under the next coefficient, and so on.

paragraphs.heading: Peeling off known roots
paragraphs.text: Sometimes you already know a root r of a degree-n polynomial P(x), perhaps from the rational root theorem. Dividing by (x − r) then factors P(x) as (x − r)Q(x), where Q(x) has degree n − 1 and the remainder must be zero. With several known roots, you can divide out one linear factor after another. A quintic with one rational root, for instance, leaves a quartic, and a formula exists for the roots of a quartic. No general algebraic method solves every quintic, though, as the Abel–Ruffini theorem shows.

paragraphs.heading: Tangent lines and error checks
paragraphs.text: Division also finds tangent lines. Divide P(x) by (x − r)², and the remainder R(x) gives the tangent line y = R(x) to the graph at x = r, whether or not r is a root. Remainders even protect data: a cyclic redundancy check uses the remainder of a polynomial division to spot errors in messages after they have been transmitted.
